questions.stem: The restorative theory of sleep proposes that sleep:
options: evolved to keep animals safe and still when activity is risky
is a waste of time that serves no biological function
occurs only when the body has run out of energy completely
allows the body and brain to repair and replenish themselves
questions.explanation: Restorative theory proposes that sleep allows recovery: tissue repair, growth and replenishing energy and brain resources. Keeping animals safe when activity is risky is the evolutionary explanation.

questions.stem: Animals that are preyed upon, such as horses, tend to sleep for short periods, while lions sleep for long periods. Which theory of sleep does this best support?
options: restorative theory
decay theory
self-determination theory
evolutionary theory
questions.explanation: Evolutionary theory proposes that sleep patterns evolved to suit each species' survival needs. Prey animals need to stay alert to danger, while predators can afford long periods of sleep.

questions.stem: Which finding best supports the restorative theory of sleep?
options: Growth hormone is released mainly during deep NREM sleep
Prey animals sleep less than predators do
Most animals sleep at the time of day when hunting is hard
Sleep keeps animals still and hidden in the dark
questions.explanation: The release of growth hormone during deep NREM sleep supports the idea that sleep allows the body to grow and repair. The other findings support the evolutionary theory.

questions.stem: The sleep-wake cycle is an example of a circadian rhythm because it:
options: occurs only once a month
changes randomly from day to day
follows a cycle of about 24 hours
repeats about every 90 minutes
questions.explanation: A circadian rhythm is a biological cycle of about 24 hours. The roughly 90-minute cycle of NREM and REM within a night is a different, shorter rhythm.

questions.stem: Which external cue has the strongest influence on keeping the sleep-wake cycle in time with the 24-hour day?
options: background noise
the time of the last meal
daylight
room temperature
questions.explanation: Light is the main external cue that keeps the circadian sleep-wake cycle aligned with day and night. Temperature, noise and meal times have much weaker effects.

questions.stem: How many stages of NREM sleep are there in the current classification?
options: four
five
three
two
questions.explanation: Current classification describes three stages of NREM sleep (N1, N2 and N3) and one stage of REM sleep. Older systems divided deep sleep into two stages, giving four NREM stages.

questions.stem: Electroencephalography (EEG) is used in sleep research to measure:
options: the rate of breathing
the electrical activity of the brain
the movement of the eyes during sleep
the tension of the muscles in the chin
questions.explanation: An EEG records brainwave patterns through electrodes on the scalp. Brainwaves change in frequency and amplitude across the sleep stages.

questions.stem: Sleep spindles and K-complexes on an EEG are characteristic of which stage?
options: NREM stage 2
NREM stage 1
NREM stage 3
REM sleep
questions.explanation: NREM stage 2 shows theta waves with sleep spindles (short bursts of fast waves) and K-complexes (large single waves). NREM stage 3 is dominated by delta waves.

questions.stem: Which stage of sleep shows mainly high-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves and is the hardest stage from which to wake someone?
options: NREM stage 3
NREM stage 1
NREM stage 2
REM sleep
questions.explanation: NREM stage 3 is deep sleep with mainly delta waves. Heart rate and breathing are at their slowest and the sleeper is hard to wake.

questions.stem: A sleeper's EEG shows fast, low-amplitude, irregular waves similar to wakefulness, but her muscles are almost completely relaxed. She is most likely in:
options: REM sleep
NREM stage 1
NREM stage 3
relaxed wakefulness
questions.explanation: REM sleep shows beta-like brainwaves similar to an alert, awake brain, yet the body's voluntary muscles are almost paralysed. In relaxed wakefulness, muscle tension would be much higher.

questions.stem: Which stage of sleep has slow rolling eye movements, theta waves and is easily interrupted, sometimes by a sudden muscle jerk?
options: NREM stage 2
NREM stage 3
REM sleep
NREM stage 1
questions.explanation: NREM stage 1 is the transition from wakefulness to sleep, with theta waves, slow rolling eye movements and easy waking. Hypnic jerks can occur in this light stage.

questions.stem: During which stage is heart rate lowest, and during which is it most irregular?
options: lowest in NREM stage 3; most irregular in REM
lowest in REM; most irregular in NREM stage 3
lowest in NREM stage 1; most irregular in NREM stage 2
lowest in NREM stage 2; most irregular in NREM stage 1
questions.explanation: Heart rate slows as NREM sleep deepens and is lowest in stage 3. In REM sleep, heart rate and breathing increase and become irregular, closer to waking levels.

questions.stem: Why is REM sleep sometimes called 'paradoxical sleep'?
options: Heart rate is very low while eye movements are completely absent
It shows delta waves even though the person is easy to wake
The brain is very active while the body is nearly paralysed
The brain is almost inactive while the muscles are very tense
questions.explanation: In REM sleep the EEG resembles that of an alert, awake brain, yet voluntary muscles are almost completely relaxed. This combination of an active brain and inactive body is the paradox.

questions.stem: Which correctly matches each sleep stage to its eye movements?
options: NREM 1: slow rolling; NREM 3: very little; REM: rapid
NREM 1: rapid; NREM 3: slow rolling; REM: very little
NREM 1: very little; NREM 3: rapid; REM: slow rolling
NREM 1: rapid; NREM 3: rapid; REM: very little
questions.explanation: Slow rolling eye movements occur in NREM stage 1, eye movements are rare in deep NREM sleep, and rapid bursts of eye movement give REM its name.

questions.stem: As a person moves from NREM stage 1 to NREM stage 3, which change occurs?
options: Eye movements become rapid and jerky
Brainwaves become slower and larger in amplitude
Brainwaves become faster and smaller in amplitude
Muscle tension increases steadily
questions.explanation: Moving deeper into NREM sleep, brainwaves slow in frequency and increase in amplitude, from theta to delta waves. Muscle tension and heart rate decrease.

questions.stem: In an adult, one complete cycle of NREM and REM sleep lasts about:
options: 24 hours
90 minutes
20 minutes
4 hours
questions.explanation: A sleep cycle lasts about 90 minutes, so an adult has about four to six cycles in a typical night. Twenty-four hours is the length of the circadian sleep-wake cycle.

questions.stem: How does the make-up of sleep cycles change across a typical night?
options: All cycles contain exactly the same amount of each stage
REM sleep occurs only in the first cycle of the night
NREM stage 3 decreases and REM periods lengthen later on
NREM stage 3 increases and REM periods shorten later in the night
questions.explanation: Early cycles contain the most deep NREM stage 3 sleep. As the night goes on, stage 3 decreases or disappears and REM periods become longer.

questions.stem: A person is woken after 7 hours of sleep and reports a long, vivid dream. In which part of the night was she most likely sleeping?
options: NREM stage 1 at the very start of the night
a short REM period in the first sleep cycle
a long REM period near the end of the night
deep NREM stage 3 at the start of the night
questions.explanation: REM periods are longest in the later part of the night, and vivid dreams are most often reported on waking from REM. Deep NREM sleep is concentrated early in the night.

questions.stem: Which of these is a common cause of sleep deprivation?
options: a consistent wake-up time
shift work
regular exercise
a dark, quiet bedroom
questions.explanation: Shift work disrupts the sleep-wake cycle by requiring people to be awake when their circadian rhythm promotes sleep. The other options are features of good sleep hygiene.

questions.stem: A nurse works rotating night shifts and struggles to sleep during the day. The main reason is that:
options: night shifts make the body need much less sleep overall
daytime sleep contains only REM and no NREM sleep
working at night removes the need for deep sleep
her sleep times clash with her circadian rhythm
questions.explanation: Her body clock promotes alertness during the day, and daylight further disrupts sleep. Shift work leaves the sleep-wake cycle out of step with the times she can sleep.

questions.stem: Drinking coffee in the evening can cause sleep deprivation because caffeine:
options: is a depressant that causes deep sleep too early
lowers heart rate so much that sleep is often interrupted
only affects sleep if taken in the morning
is a stimulant that increases alertness and delays sleep
questions.explanation: Caffeine is a stimulant drug that increases arousal and can make it harder to fall asleep and stay asleep. Its effects can last for several hours after it is consumed.

questions.stem: Worrying about final exams keeps Lily awake late into the night. This cause of sleep deprivation is best described as:
options: a stressor
shift work
the sleep environment
a drug
questions.explanation: Stressors increase physiological and cognitive arousal, making it harder to fall and stay asleep. The sleep environment refers to features such as light, noise and temperature.

questions.stem: Which is an effect of acute sleep deprivation?
options: chronic insomnia
slower reflexes
obesity
heart disease
questions.explanation: Acute sleep deprivation, from a short period of lost sleep, affects mood, attention, reflex speed and vision. Obesity and heart disease are linked to chronic sleep deprivation.

questions.stem: After one night without sleep, Max is irritable, keeps losing focus in class and misses a ball he would usually catch. These effects show acute sleep deprivation affecting:
options: growth, memory storage and vision
insomnia, obesity and heart rate
mood, attention and reflex speed
weight, heart health and anxiety
questions.explanation: Irritability reflects mood, losing focus reflects attention, and missing the ball reflects slower reflexes. Weight and heart health are linked to chronic deprivation.

questions.stem: Which effect is linked to chronic rather than acute sleep deprivation?
options: increased risk of heart disease
blurred vision the next day
irritability the next morning
brief lapses in attention
questions.explanation: Chronic sleep deprivation, over weeks or longer, is associated with heart disease, obesity, insomnia and anxiety. Next-day effects on vision, mood and attention are acute effects.

questions.stem: Which is the most accurate statement about chronic sleep deprivation and obesity?
options: Long-term lack of sleep is linked to a higher risk of obesity
Long-term lack of sleep always causes obesity in every person
Long-term lack of sleep reduces appetite and leads to weight loss
Long-term lack of sleep affects weight only in older adults
questions.explanation: Research links chronic sleep deprivation with a greater risk of obesity, partly through changes in appetite-regulating hormones. It increases risk rather than causing obesity in everyone.

questions.stem: A driver who has slept only four hours drifts across a lane because he briefly lost focus and reacted late. Which effects of acute sleep deprivation does this show?
options: improved vision and a better mood
reduced attention and slower reflex speed
insomnia and anxiety about driving
heart disease and long-term obesity
questions.explanation: Lapses in attention and slower reactions are effects of acute sleep deprivation, which is why fatigue is a major road safety risk.

questions.stem: In psychology, the term sleep hygiene refers to:
options: medication prescribed for insomnia
habits that help a person sleep well
the stages of NREM and REM sleep
washing bedding to prevent illness
questions.explanation: Sleep hygiene is the set of behaviours and environmental conditions that promote good sleep, such as consistent sleep times and a dark, quiet bedroom.

questions.stem: Which is the best sleep hygiene advice about electronic devices?
options: Keep the phone on the pillow to hear any messages
Turn screen brightness up to reduce eye strain at night
Stop using screens for a period before bedtime
Use screens until falling asleep to relax the brain
questions.explanation: Screens can increase arousal and their light can delay sleepiness. Stopping device use before bed and keeping devices out of the bedroom are common recommendations.

questions.stem: Kate goes to bed at 9 pm on school nights but stays up until 2 am and sleeps until noon on weekends. Which sleep hygiene technique should she apply?
options: keeping a consistent sleep pattern every day
using her phone in bed to wind down
napping for several hours each weekend afternoon
drinking coffee after dinner to stay alert
questions.explanation: Large shifts in sleep times on weekends disrupt the circadian rhythm. Going to bed and waking at similar times every day helps keep the sleep-wake cycle stable.

questions.stem: Which feature describes a healthy sleep environment?
options: lit by a television left on
used for study and gaming
dark, quiet and cool
bright, warm and noisy
questions.explanation: A healthy sleep environment is dark, quiet, comfortable and cool, and the bed is used mainly for sleep. Light, noise and activities such as gaming increase arousal.

questions.stem: What was the aim of He et al. (2020)?
options: to test whether daylight resets the circadian rhythm of travellers
to test whether limiting phone use before bed improves sleep
to test whether shift work causes heart disease in nurses over many years
to test whether caffeine before bed reduces deep NREM sleep in adults
questions.explanation: He et al. investigated the effect of restricting mobile phone use before bedtime on sleep, pre-sleep arousal, mood and working memory in university students.

questions.stem: In He et al. (2020), what were participants in the intervention group asked to do?
options: stop using their phones completely for the four weeks
go to bed 30 minutes earlier with their phones
not use their phones for 30 minutes before bedtime
use their phones for 30 minutes in bed each night
questions.explanation: The intervention group avoided phone use in the 30 minutes before their usual bedtime for four weeks. The control group was given no instructions about phone use.

questions.stem: He et al. (2020) randomly allocated 38 students who used their phones in bed and slept poorly to an intervention or control group. Which findings did they report for the intervention group?
options: no change in sleep but improved working memory only
shorter sleep but lower pre-sleep arousal
faster sleep onset, longer sleep and better working memory
longer time to fall asleep but better mood and working memory
questions.explanation: After four weeks of restricting bedtime phone use, the intervention group fell asleep faster, slept longer, reported better sleep quality, lower pre-sleep arousal, more positive affect and improved working memory.

questions.stem: Which is a valid limitation of He et al. (2020)?
options: Participants were not randomly allocated to groups
Sleep was measured only with EEG in a sleep laboratory
The small sample of students limits generalisability
No control group was used for comparison
questions.explanation: The study used a small sample of university students who slept poorly, and sleep was measured by self-report rather than objective measures. It did use random allocation and a control group.

questions.stem: What was a key contribution of He et al. (2020) to psychology?
options: It proved that phones cause chronic insomnia in all adults
It showed that working memory is unaffected by sleep quality
It identified the stages of NREM sleep for the first time
It tested a sleep hygiene technique experimentally
questions.explanation: As a randomised controlled trial, it gave evidence that restricting phone use before bed can improve sleep and related outcomes. Its small pilot sample means it supports, rather than proves, the technique.
